food.text: The earliest credible evidence of coffee drinking dates to the middle of the 15th century in Yemen, where coffee was already used in Sufi monasteries. Sufis drank it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions.
After the rise of Islam, Arab traders came to control the flow of spices through the Levant to Venetian merchants bound for Europe. This dominance lasted until the Seljuk Turks rose to power in 1090.

According to historic Arabic cookbooks, grains were mainly turned into porridge and pasta-type dishes in Arab cuisine until the 12th century. Two kinds of pasta were known: itriya, a short dry noodle of Greek origin, and rishta, a hand-cut fresh noodle of Persian origin.

According to a translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript, coffee's use spread from Arabia Felix, the old name for Yemen, north to the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. From there it reached the larger cities of Cairo, Damascus, Baghdad and Constantinople.

The 14th-century traveller Ibn Battuta visited Aden and described its Cisterns of Tawila. These reservoirs collected rainwater for the sole purpose of supplying the city's citizens with drinking water.
Under the Rasulid dynasty, Aden's kings were merchants themselves. They dug wells and built schools, and enacted laws and regulations to codify trade, helping the port city flourish commercially.
By the 13th century, Turkic-style tutmaj and salma noodles had also entered Arab cuisine. These joined the porridge and pasta dishes that Arab cooks had long made from grains.

The writer Abd al-Qadir al-Jaziri, who compiled a history of coffee in 1587, reported that a sheikh named Jamal-al-Din al-Dhabhani, the mufti of Aden, was the first to adopt coffee drinking. This was said to have happened around 1454, and al-Dhabhani died in 1470.

Rasulid sultan al-Afdal Abbas ruled Yemen from 1363 to 1377 and compiled a compendium called Fusul majmua fi'l-anwa' wa 'l-zuru' wa 'l-hisad. It covered practical matters such as crops and harvests, alongside topics of intellectual interest and entertainment.

art.text: In 1130, the Isma'ili Queen Arwa al-Sulayhi restored much of the Great Mosque of Sanaa in Yemen, adding sculpted ceilings to its eastern, western, and northern wings. Her restoration also included building the mosque's western minaret.

Around 1200, the Great Mosque of Zabid in Yemen was rebuilt under the Ayyubid dynasty, gaining most of its present form. Its brick minaret, built at this time, is one of the oldest preserved minarets in Yemen.

By the 14th century, the Yemeni city of Zabid was said to contain between 230 and 240 mosques, according to the local writer al-Khazraji. Even today, Zabid reportedly has the highest concentration of mosques in Yemen.

Rasulid sultans, who ruled Yemen from 1229 to 1454, built numerous mosques and madrasas across cities including Ta'izz. Most of these buildings were inspired by architectural models from Egypt and Syria, breaking with the older Yemeni style of architecture.

The western minaret built during Queen Arwa al-Sulayhi's 1130 restoration of the Great Mosque of Sanaa closely resembles minarets from mosques built in Cairo around the same period. This reflects her close ties to the Fatimid dynasty in Egypt.
The minaret built during the Ayyubid rebuilding of the Great Mosque of Zabid around 1200 has an octagonal shaft. It is distinguished by its decorative brickwork.

Under the Rasulid dynasty (1229 to 1454), the capital of Yemen moved to Ta'izz, but Zabid remained the rulers' winter residence. The city reached its peak in this period, boasting more palaces, gardens, and religious institutions than any other city in Yemen.

Among the Rasulid dynasty's most well-known monuments are the thirteenth-century al-Muzaffar Mosque and the fourteenth-century Ashrafiyya Mosque, both built in Ta'izz. These fine buildings were part of a wider effort by Rasulid rulers to embellish the city.

As part of the same 1130 restoration, the wooden ceilings of the Great Mosque of Sanaa were carved and painted rather than left plain. This decorative craftsmanship was part of Queen Arwa al-Sulayhi's broader renovation of the mosque.

In 1492, the Tahirid dynasty carried out further restoration of the Great Mosque of Zabid, adding to centuries of modification since its Ayyubid rebuilding around 1200. The mosque follows a hypostyle plan with a central courtyard, echoing the classic early Arab mosque design.

Between about 1236 and 1438, Rasulid sultans struck coins at mints across Yemen, each marked with its own symbol. Aden's coins bore a fish, Zabid's a bird, Ta'izz's a seated man, and al-Mahjam's a lion.

war.text: The Qarmatians were a radical Isma'ili group that held power in eastern Arabia and became known for raiding caravans of pilgrims travelling to Mecca. Their rule was later ended by an uprising backed by the Abbasids and the Seljuks.

In 1068, Abu al-Bahlul al-Awwam revolted against the Qarmatians and seized the island of Awal. He defeated the Qarmatian army and its allies from Banu Amir and some of Abd al-Qays in a fierce naval battle.

The Uyunids were a local Arab dynasty from the tribe of Bani Abd al-Qays. Their chief, Abdullah bin Ali Al Uyuni, allied with the Abbasids and Seljuks and, with their support, quickly conquered Awal and Qatif, exiled Qatif's new ruler Yahya bin Al-Ayash, and invaded the Qarmatian stronghold of Hofuf. Uyunid and Seljuk forces besieged Hofuf for seven whole years until it fell, and the Qarmatian state fell with it. He then founded the Uyunid Emirate, which pledged allegiance to the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad.
In 1078, Yahya ibn Ayyash, chief of Banu Muharib of Abd al-Qays, rose up against the Qarmatians. He expelled their officials from Qatif and extended his influence to the island of Awal.

After his naval victory, Abu al-Bahlul crowned himself Emir of the island. He could not beat Yahya bin Abbas, the new leader of Qatif, and the island soon came under their control again, with Abu al-Bahlul killed in the process.

Al-Uyuni killed a Seljuk general in an instance of friendly fire, and Sultan Malik-Shah I ordered the governor of Kerman to raise an army against the Uyunids in Al-Ahsa. Seeing the huge difference in numbers, Al-Uyuni submitted and offered to help the Seljuks invade Oman, hoping to minimize Seljuk influence in his emirate.

literature.text: Nabati is a vernacular Arabic poetry from the Arabian Peninsula, set apart from poetry written by the strict rules of classical literary Arabic. It is often called "the people's poetry" or "Bedouin poetry". The medieval historian Ibn Khaldun referred to examples of the form in his Muqaddimah, first published in 1377.

Bedouin poets of Arabia composed verse similar in structure, theme, metre and rhyme to the works of Imru' al-Qais and other pre-Islamic poets. These qasida set the classical standard for hundreds of years. Even verse by illiterate Bedouin masters stayed close in spirit and language to these examples.

Ibn Arabi, a scholar and poet from al-Andalus, had 850 works attributed to him, though only 700 are considered authentic and only 400 survive. He began writing his Meccan Illuminations while living in Mecca for three years after arriving for the Hajj in 1202.

The Romance of Antar, long handed down by oral tradition only, grew to immense proportions and was later published in 32 volumes at Cairo. Sultan Mehmed II ordered it translated into Turkish in 1477. Traditional storytellers still recite it in Arab coffee houses.

The original Bedouin poets transmitted nabati poems orally, and writing them down was a later innovation. Poems were recited at gatherings where people drank coffee together and shared verse. Tribes wrote, recited and memorized pieces honoring their own lineage.

Illustrated copies of the Maqamat al-Hariri began to appear from the early 13th century, since editions in al-Hariri's lifetime had no pictures. One of the earliest and best known is by al-Wasiti, dated 1236, now in the Bibliothèque nationale de France.

Al-Zamakhshari began writing his Quran commentary Al-Kashshaf in 1132, while residing in Mecca, and finished it in two years. It is widely considered the first commentary focused on rhetoric, drawing on al-Jurjani's idea that the Quran's miracle lies in the structure and arrangement of its words.

Ibn al-Farid's greengrocer story begins when a greengrocer, seen washing wrongly outside a madrasa, told him he would be enlightened only in Mecca and gave him a vision of it. Ibn al-Farid left at once and stayed in Mecca for fifteen years. He returned to Cairo because he heard the same greengrocer calling him back to attend his funeral, and he found the man on the point of death. Ibn al-Farid later wrote that at the greengrocer's funeral a "great green bird" came down and "gobbled up his corpse".

More than a hundred manuscripts of the Maqamat al-Hariri are known, but only thirteen are illustrated. A first phase of illustrated copies, made between 1200 and 1256 in areas between Syria and Iraq, was followed by a 50-year gap corresponding to the Mongol invasions of Persia, Mesopotamia and the Levant, including the Siege of Baghdad in 1258. Production resumed from around 1300 to 1337 during the Egyptian Mamluk period, probably centered around Cairo.

Ibn al-Mujawir's travel chronicle describes cities, commerce and social customs of southern Arabia in the early 13th century. In Aden he recorded the port's taxes, markets, currency, weights and measures, and he also noted local tales and myths.
Al-Hariri's Maqamat was translated into Hebrew by Yehuda Alharizi, who died in 1225. His version was a major influence on Alharizi's own maqamat, the Tahkemoni.

politics.text: The Rasulid dynasty, a Sunni Yemeni family, ruled Yemen from 1229 to 1454. In the year 1454 the last Rasulid sultan, al-Mas'ud Abu al-Qasim, gave up his throne to az-Zafir Amir bin Tahir and withdrew to Mecca. The new ruling clan governed Yemen as the Tahirids until 1517.

The Zaydi imamate of Yemen was a blend of religious and political rule that began in 897 and lasted until the republican revolution in 1962. From the 11th to the early 17th centuries, the imams were usually not the sons of the former imam. Instead the office circulated among the various Rassid branches.

Medieval Yemen was a patchwork of small dynasties. Among the better known were the Sulayhids in the southern highlands from 1047 to 1138, the Zuray'ids in Aden from 1080 to 1174, and the Hatimids in San'a from 1098 to 1174. While the Fatimid state was influential, part of the population converted to Isma'ili Shi'ism.

Beginning in 1174, the family of Salah al-Din ibn Ayyub (Saladin) conquered Yemen. A series of dynasties then exercised some control there for roughly 400 years: the Ayyubids, Rasulids, Tahirids and Mamluks, until the Ottoman Empire took the Yemeni Tihama in 1538.

In 1083 the Sulayhid heir al-Mukarram Ahmad ended the rule of the Banu Ma'n in Aden and installed two brothers, Al-Abbas and Al-Msaod. Al-Abbas handled trade with the interior from Ta'kar, while Al-Msaod handled shipping from the castle al-Khadra. About 100,000 dinars were paid in tribute each year.

Bahrain's pearl fisheries built up great wealth. After Hormuz took Bahrain and Qatif in 1320, its rulers did not seem to hold the islands firmly. During the 14th century neighbouring powers disputed Bahrain because they sought tribute from that pearl wealth.

In 1350 the Rasulid sultan al-Mujahid Ali went on a pilgrimage to Mecca. There he was captured by the Egyptian Mamluks, who tended to increase their influence in the Hijaz and holy cities. He was held prisoner in Egypt for a year.

Sultan an-Nasir Ahmad, who reigned from 1401 to 1424, revived the Rasulid dynasty's declining fortunes and even received gifts from distant China. After his death in 1424 the dynasty fell into a period of upheaval and weakness, aggravated by the outbreak of the plague.

After 1110 the Zurayids led an independent rule of more than 60 years in Aden, bolstered by international trade. Chronicles mention luxury goods such as textiles, perfume and porcelain, coming from places like North Africa, Egypt, Iraq, Oman, Kirman and China.

Rasulid rulers were also men of letters. Al-Afdal Abbas, who reigned 1363 to 1377, wrote an extensive compendium, and his son al-Ashraf Isma'il, who reigned 1377 to 1401, authored a general history of Yemen. Coins were struck by all the sultans, with symbols for each mint: fish for Aden, bird for Zabid, sitting man for Ta'izz, and lion for al-Mahjam.

The Sulayhid queen Arwa demanded tribute from the Zurayids of Aden, but their sons ceased to pay it after their fathers Zuray and Al-Msaod were killed during the 1110 siege of Zabid. The Zurayids were worsted by a Sulayhid expedition, and Arwa agreed to halve the tribute to 50,000 dinars per year. They failed to pay again and were forced to yield once more, so it was cut to 25,000. Later they stopped paying even that, since Sulayhid power was on the wane.

philosophy.text: In late medieval Yemen, Jewish thinkers built what became known as "Jewish Ismailism". It adapted a few Ismaili doctrines about cosmology, prophecy and hermeneutics to Judaism.

Natan'el al-Fayyumi of Yemen wrote the Bustan al-Uqul ("Garden of Intellects") in the twelfth century. Like the Ismailis, he argued that God sent different prophets to various nations, bringing legislation suited to each nation's particular temperament.

Ismaili doctrine holds that a single universal religious truth lies at the root of the different religions. Some Jews accepted this pluralism and saw Muhammad as a legitimate prophet, though not a Jewish one, sent to preach to the Arabs. Others rejected the idea entirely.
Hoter ben Shlomo was a scholar and philosopher in Yemen. He was heavily influenced by Nethanel ben al-Fayyumi, Maimonides, Saadia Gaon and al-Ghazali.

The Epistle of the Brethren of Purity is linked to Ismailism, which suggests it was adopted as one of the main sources of Jewish Ismailism in late medieval Yemenite Judaism. Its influence on Yemenite Jewish philosophers and authors is attested for the period 1150–1550.

Two Yemenite philosophical midrashim were written in 1420–1430: the Midrash ha-hefez ("Midrash of Desire") by Zechariah ha-Rofé, also called Yahya al-Tabib, and the Siraj al-'uqul ("Lamp of Intellects") by Hoter ben Solomon. Both contain traces of Brethren of Purity doctrines and their numerology.

Yaqut al-Hamawi (d. 1229) quoted Ibn al-Kalbi's Book of Idols extensively in his Ma'jum al-buldan. This let Julius Wellhausen work with the text through Yaqut's citations before its main manuscript was discovered.

culture.text: Eastern Arabia, and Bahrain in particular, became a principal centre of knowledge for hundreds of years, stretching from the early days of Islam to the 18th century. Its philosophers were highly esteemed.

Fourteenth-century Arab genealogists shared a general consensus that Arabs were of three kinds. Arab traditions about the origins and classification of the Arabian tribes were based on biblical genealogy.

Sheikh Maitham Al Bahrani, a 13th-century mystic who died in 1299, was among the esteemed philosophers of eastern Arabia. His mosque and tomb can still be visited on the outskirts of Manama, near the district of Mahooz.

Rashid al-Din Hamadani, who died in 1318, wrote in his Jāmiʾ al-Tawārīkh that Buddhist idols could be found in the Kaaba. He also wrote that both Arabs and some Persians on the peninsula saw themselves as students of the Buddha.
A thirteenth-century Islamic miniature shows Muhammad destroying Hindu and Buddhist idols at the Kaaba, one of several Islamic sources depicting a Buddhist presence in pre-Islamic Arabia.

Medieval Muslim scholars kept trying to describe the religion of pre-Islamic Arabia after Ibn al-Kalbi. Among them was Shahrastani, who died in 1153. Such writers built on earlier works like the Book of Idols, though many historians now doubt that book's reliability.
